topic: Balance training after 60: small habits that prevent falls

slides.headline: Balance is trainable at any age
slides.sub: Small daily habits that help you stay steady on your feet.

slides.title: Balance responds to practice
slides.body: Balance relies on your muscles, joints, eyes and inner ear working together. Like strength, it tends to improve when you challenge it regularly, and research suggests exercise can reduce falls in older adults.

slides.title: Habit 1: stand on one leg
slides.body: While the kettle boils, hold the bench and lift one foot. Aim for 10 to 30 seconds each side. As it gets easier, lighten your grip to fingertips, then let your hand hover.

slides.title: Habit 2: sit to stand, slowly
slides.body: Stand up from a chair without using your hands, then sit down slowly. Ten times, once or twice a day. Leg strength is a big part of catching yourself if you trip.

slides.title: Habit 3: make your home easier
slides.body: Good lighting on the way to the bathroom at night, no loose rugs, and a clear path down the hallway. Simple changes like these are easy to overlook.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See your GP or physio if you've had a fall, feel dizzy or unsteady when you stand up, notice new weakness in your legs, or find yourself avoiding walks because you're worried about falling.

slides.headline: Want a balance plan that fits?
slides.body: Our Milton and Sunnybank physios assess your strength, balance and walking, then build a short home program you can actually stick to. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Balance isn't something you simply lose with age. It's a skill, and it responds to practice.

Your muscles, joints, eyes and inner ear all work together to keep you steady. Research suggests regular exercise can reduce falls in older adults, and small daily habits add up: standing on one leg while the kettle boils, sit to stands, and clearing loose rugs at home.

If you've had a fall, feel dizzy when you stand, or are avoiding walks because you're worried about falling, have a chat with your GP or physio. If you have a chronic condition, ask your GP whether a chronic condition management plan suits you. It can give a Medicare rebate for up to 5 allied health visits a year, and there's usually a gap fee.

topic: A 5-minute hip and lower back mobility routine

slides.headline: Five minutes, five moves, looser hips
slides.sub: A simple routine for stiff hips and a tight lower back.

slides.title: 1 minute: cat-cow
slides.body: On hands and knees, slowly round your back up, then let it dip down as you look forward. Move within a comfortable range and breathe steadily. About eight slow rounds is plenty.

slides.title: 1 minute: knee rocks
slides.body: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat. Let both knees drop gently to one side, then the other, keeping your shoulders relaxed on the floor. It's an easy way to ease morning stiffness.

slides.title: 1 minute: half-kneeling hip stretch
slides.body: Kneel on one knee with the other foot forward. Tuck your tailbone slightly and shift forward until you feel a stretch at the front of the hip. Thirty seconds each side.

slides.title: 2 minutes: glute stretch and rest
slides.body: Lying down, cross one ankle over the other knee and draw your legs towards you for 30 seconds each side. Finish in child's pose, breathing slowly into your lower back for a minute.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Get assessed if pain spreads down a leg with pins and needles or weakness, or if you notice numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes, fever, or pain after a fall.

slides.headline: Stiff most mornings?
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess how your hips and back move, may use hands-on care alongside exercise, and send you home with a routine that suits you. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Five minutes. Five moves. Looser hips and a happier lower back.

Stiffness through the hips and lower back is common, especially after long days sitting or a big weekend. Try this: one minute of cat-cow, one minute of knee rocks, a minute of half-kneeling hip stretches, then a glute stretch and a minute in child's pose. Move gently and within comfort.

slides.headline: Pregnancy massage: what to expect
slides.sub: Comfort, positioning and a few things to mention first.

slides.title: Is it OK in pregnancy?
slides.body: For most people with an uncomplicated pregnancy, massage from a trained therapist is generally considered fine. It's worth letting your midwife, GP or obstetrician know, especially if you have any complications.

slides.title: How you'll be positioned
slides.body: From the second trimester, lying flat on your back for long periods can feel uncomfortable. Side-lying with pillows between your knees and under the bump is common, and you can change position anytime.

slides.title: What it can help with
slides.body: Many people find massage eases tight shoulders, a sore lower back and heavy, tired legs. It's a helpful way to relax and feel more comfortable, alongside staying active in ways that suit you.

slides.title: Tell your therapist about
slides.body: How many weeks along you are, any complications, swelling that's new or only on one side, recent pain, and what feels good. Pressure is always adjustable, so speak up if anything feels off.

slides.title: When to check with your care team
slides.body: Contact your midwife or doctor promptly for bleeding, sudden swelling of the face or hands, a severe headache, calf pain or swelling in one leg, or reduced baby movements.

topic: Rehab after knee replacement: what the first 12 weeks look like

slides.headline: Your first 12 weeks with a new knee
slides.sub: A rough guide to what rehab usually looks like.

slides.title: Weeks 0 to 2: early movement
slides.body: Most people are up walking with an aid soon after surgery. The focus is gently bending and straightening the knee, managing swelling, and short, frequent walks around the house.

slides.title: Weeks 2 to 6: build the bend
slides.body: Stitches or clips usually come out and exercises progress. Working on knee bend and getting it fully straight matters now. Swelling and stiffness are normal and often worse by evening.

slides.title: Weeks 6 to 12: getting stronger
slides.body: Many people move from a stick to walking unaided, tackle stairs more normally, and start an exercise bike or hydrotherapy if cleared. Thigh and hip strength become the main focus.

slides.title: Recovery keeps going after 12 weeks
slides.body: Some swelling and stiffness can linger for months, and that's common. Many people keep improving for a year or more, so steady, regular exercise pays off well beyond the early stage.

slides.title: When to call your surgeon or GP
slides.body: Increasing redness, heat or discharge around the wound, fever, calf pain or swelling, or a sharp jump in pain. Sudden shortness of breath needs urgent care, so call 000.

slides.headline: Want help with the next stage?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios progress your rehab in line with your surgeon's guidelines, with clear goals for each stage. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
New knee? Here's roughly what the first 12 weeks look like.

Weeks 0 to 2 are about gentle bending and straightening, managing swelling and short, frequent walks. Weeks 2 to 6 build the bend, and getting the knee fully straight matters. From about week 6, many people move off the stick, manage stairs more normally and focus on thigh and hip strength.

Everyone's timeline is a little different, and swelling and stiffness can hang around for months. Many people keep improving for a year or more.

Call your surgeon or GP about increasing wound redness or discharge, fever, or calf pain or swelling. Sudden shortness of breath needs urgent care, so call 000.

topic: Pilates for golfers: rotation without the pain

slides.headline: Stiff swing? Check your mid-back
slides.sub: Pilates ideas to rotate more freely through your whole body.

slides.title: Rotation should be shared
slides.body: A smooth golf swing spreads rotation through the hips, mid-back and shoulders. When one area is stiff, another often picks up the slack, and for many golfers that's the lower back.

slides.title: Open up your mid-back
slides.body: Try open books: lie on your side, knees bent, arms together in front. Rotate the top arm open as you breathe out, following it with your eyes. Eight slow reps each side.

slides.title: Let your hips turn too
slides.body: Lying on your back, let one knee fall out and back in, then try seated hip rotations. Hips that turn freely take load off the lower back through the backswing and follow-through.

slides.title: Control, not just range
slides.body: Pilates work like side planks, the saw and single-leg exercises on the reformer builds control through the trunk, so you can turn with speed without losing your posture.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: If pain lingers for more than a couple of weeks, wakes you at night, or travels down an arm or leg with pins and needles, have it assessed before ramping up your practice.

slides.headline: Want a golf-specific program?
slides.body: Our clinical Pilates team assesses how you rotate, then builds a program around your swing, on the mat or reformer. Book online — link in bio.

Stiff swing and a sore lower back after 18 holes? Look a little higher up.

topic: Neck pain after a car accident (whiplash)

slides.headline: Sore neck after a car accident?
slides.sub: What's common, what helps, and when to get checked.

slides.title: Delayed stiffness is common
slides.body: Neck pain and stiffness after a car accident often appear hours or even a day or two later. That delay is normal, and most people improve steadily over the following weeks.

slides.title: When to get checked first
slides.body: See a doctor or go to the emergency department if you have severe neck pain, numbness or weakness in the arms, dizziness, trouble swallowing or speaking, or a bad headache.

slides.title: Keep gently moving
slides.body: Current guidelines favour staying active over resting in a collar. Gentle neck turns, shoulder rolls and short walks within comfort help things settle. Heat can ease tight muscles.

slides.title: Build up gradually
slides.body: As pain eases, add gentle strengthening for the neck and upper back and return to driving and work bit by bit. A small flare-up along the way is common and usually settles.

slides.title: Claiming through CTP in NSW
slides.body: If you've lodged a CTP claim, bring your claim number and insurer details. We liaise with your insurer about treatment and progress, though approval decisions rest with them.

topic: Talking to your therapist about pressure

slides.headline: Too hard? Too soft? Say so.
slides.sub: How to talk about pressure so your massage actually helps.

slides.title: Myth: harder is always better
slides.body: Deeper pressure isn't automatically more effective. Many people get the most out of firm but comfortable pressure that lets muscles relax, rather than bracing through every stroke.

slides.title: Use a simple 0 to 10 scale
slides.body: Tell your therapist where you are on a scale of 0 to 10. Around 5 to 7 is often comfortable and useful for most people. If you're holding your breath, it's too much.

slides.title: Speak up anytime
slides.body: You can ask for more pressure, less pressure or a different area at any point. Good therapists check in regularly, but you don't need to wait to be asked. It's your session.

slides.title: Mention what's going on
slides.body: Let them know about recent injuries, bruising easily, pregnancy, skin sensitivity or areas you'd rather avoid. It helps your therapist choose pressure and techniques that suit you.

slides.title: What's normal afterwards
slides.body: Mild tenderness for a day or two is common after firmer work. Heavy bruising or pain that keeps getting worse isn't expected, so let your therapist know so they can adjust next time.

slides.headline: Book a session that suits you
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists tailor pressure to you and work alongside our physios when you're also doing rehab. Book online — link in bio.

topic: What happens at your first chiropractic visit

slides.headline: What a first chiro visit looks like
slides.sub: What happens, how long it takes and what to bring.

slides.title: Step 1: a proper chat
slides.body: Your chiropractor asks about your symptoms, how they started, your health history and your goals. Bring any recent scans or reports. The first visit usually takes a bit longer than follow-ups.

slides.title: Step 2: an assessment
slides.body: They'll look at how you move, check joint range and muscle strength, and may test reflexes and sensation. This also helps pick up anything that needs a different kind of care.

slides.title: Step 3: a plan you agree on
slides.body: You'll get a clear explanation of what's likely going on and a suggested plan. It may include hands-on care, soft tissue work and exercises. Ask questions, and you can say no to anything.

slides.title: About adjustments
slides.body: Adjustments are one tool, not the whole plan. Your chiropractor will explain what's involved and ask for your consent first. If you'd prefer gentler techniques, just say so.

slides.title: Some soreness afterwards is common
slides.body: Mild stiffness or achiness for a day or so is common after a first session. Keep moving gently. If anything feels unusual or keeps getting worse, contact the clinic.

slides.headline: Why pregnancy can make your pelvis ache
slides.sub: What pelvic girdle pain is and simple ways to ease it.

slides.title: What it feels like
slides.body: Pelvic girdle pain often shows up at the front over the pubic bone, at the back near the dimples, or both. Rolling over in bed, stairs and standing on one leg can be tricky.

slides.title: Keep your knees together
slides.body: Get in and out of the car with your knees together, swinging both legs in at once. In bed, roll with your knees together, and try a pillow between your knees at night.

slides.title: Pace, don't stop
slides.body: Staying active usually helps. Break up long walks, take stairs one step at a time, avoid wide steps or straddling positions, and sit down to put on pants and shoes.

slides.title: Treatment can help
slides.body: Physiotherapy often includes exercises for the hips and trunk, advice on daily tasks, hands-on care and sometimes a support belt. For most people, it eases after the baby arrives.

slides.title: When to check with your care team
slides.body: Contact your midwife or doctor promptly for bleeding, fever, contractions, reduced baby movements, or severe, constant pain that doesn't change with position. These are uncommon, but always worth checking.

slides.headline: Get support this pregnancy
slides.body: Our Sunnybank and Milton physios assess what's aggravating your pelvis and give practical strategies for work, sleep and getting around. Book online — link in bio.

slides.headline: Over 50 and new to Pilates?
slides.sub: Five common questions, answered before your first session.

slides.title: Do I need to be flexible?
slides.body: No. Pilates builds flexibility and control over time, and exercises are adapted to where you are now. Stiff hips, tight hamstrings and creaky knees are all very workable starting points.

slides.title: Is it OK with sore joints?
slides.body: Usually, yes. Clinical Pilates starts with an assessment, so exercises can be adjusted around sore knees, backs or shoulders. Let us know about past injuries, operations or health conditions.

slides.title: Is it only about the core?
slides.body: Not at all. Good programs include leg strength, balance and upper body work, which matter more as we get older. Current guidelines recommend strength training for adults of all ages.

slides.title: How often should I go?
slides.body: Once or twice a week is a good starting point. Consistency counts for more than intensity, so pick a time that fits your routine and build up gradually over a few months.

topic: Foam rolling vs massage: do you need both?

slides.headline: Foam roller or massage? Maybe both
slides.sub: What each one does well and how to use them together.

slides.title: What foam rolling does well
slides.body: It's quick, cheap and you can do it daily. Many people find a few minutes of rolling helps them feel looser before training or after a long day at the desk.

slides.title: What massage adds
slides.body: A remedial massage therapist can assess and target specific areas, adjust pressure as they go, and reach spots that are hard to roll, like the neck and between the shoulder blades.

slides.title: Myth: roll until it hurts
slides.body: Rolling harder isn't more helpful. Aim for firm but comfortable pressure, about 30 to 60 seconds per area, and breathe slowly. Skip bony spots and go gently around the lower back.

slides.title: Neither replaces exercise
slides.body: Both can help you feel looser for a while, but strength work, mobility and gradual training are what build your body's capacity over time. Think of them as helpful add-ons.

slides.title: A simple way to combine them
slides.body: Roll briefly most days, especially calves, quads and upper back. Book a massage when an area keeps tightening up or you're in a heavy training block, and mention your routine.

slides.headline: Want a hands-on reset?
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists can show you where to roll at home and work alongside our physios if you're also doing rehab. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Tennis and golf: shoulder care for weekend players

slides.headline: Keep your shoulder in the weekend game
slides.sub: Four shoulder tips for tennis and golf players.

slides.title: Warm up before the first swing
slides.body: Five minutes of arm circles, band pull-aparts and easy swings or rallying helps your shoulder get ready. Many weekend players go straight to full power, which shoulders often dislike.

slides.title: Build load across the week
slides.body: A sudden jump, like a long tournament after weeks off, is a common trigger for sore shoulders. Where you can, play a little more often rather than a lot all at once.

slides.title: Strengthen the rotator cuff
slides.body: Side-lying external rotations and band rows, two or three times a week, help the shoulder handle repeated swings. Start light, three sets of 10 to 15, and build up gradually.

slides.title: Use your whole body
slides.body: Power in a serve or drive comes from the legs and trunk. If your hips and mid-back don't turn freely, the shoulder often ends up working harder. Mobility work for those areas helps.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain that stops you sleeping on that side, weakness lifting the arm, a sudden pop with bruising, pins and needles down the arm, or pain that lasts more than a few weeks.

slides.headline: Keep playing with confidence
slides.body: Our Milton and Sunnybank physios assess your shoulder and the demands of your sport, then build a plan to keep you on the court or course. Book online — link in bio.

And remember power comes from the legs and trunk, so stiff hips or mid-back can leave the shoulder doing extra work.

topic: Jaw tension, stress and neck tightness

slides.headline: Clenching your jaw without noticing?
slides.sub: How jaw tension, stress and a tight neck often go together.

slides.title: They're closely linked
slides.body: The jaw, neck and upper shoulders share muscles and nerves, so tension in one often shows up in the others. Stress, long screen days and poor sleep can all add to it.

slides.title: Check your resting jaw
slides.body: Right now, are your teeth touching? At rest, lips gently closed, teeth apart, tongue resting on the roof of your mouth. Set a phone reminder to check in a few times a day.

slides.title: Loosen the neck and shoulders
slides.body: Every hour or so, roll your shoulders, gently tuck your chin and turn your head side to side. Short breaks from the screen often help more than one long stretch at night.

slides.title: Wind down before bed
slides.body: Slow breathing, a warm shower, or gentle circles with your fingertips on the muscle in front of your ear can help your jaw relax. Many people clench more during stressful weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See your dentist or GP if your jaw locks, clicks painfully or makes eating hard, or if you have new severe headaches, facial numbness, or pain after an injury.

slides.headline: Tight neck and jaw lately?
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess your neck, jaw and upper back, may use gentle hands-on care alongside exercise, and liaise with your dentist when needed. Book online — link in bio.

slides.headline: Standing desks: helpful or hype?
slides.sub: What they're good for, and what they can't do on their own.

slides.title: The short answer: somewhat helpful
slides.body: A standing desk makes it easier to change position through the day, which many people find more comfortable. On its own, though, it's not a solution for back or neck pain.

slides.title: Standing all day isn't the goal
slides.body: Long spells of standing still bring their own aches in the feet, legs and lower back. The aim is variety: sit, stand, walk and move, rather than swapping one static posture for another.

slides.title: Set it up well
slides.body: When standing, keep the desk around elbow height, with the screen at about eye level and an arm's length away. Shift your weight often, and try a soft mat or supportive shoes.

slides.title: A simple rhythm to try
slides.body: Change position every 30 to 45 minutes. Stand for calls, sit for focused work, and take a short walk every hour. A reminder on your phone or watch makes it much easier to stick to.

slides.title: Movement matters more than furniture
slides.body: Regular activity outside work, like walking, strength training or Pilates, tends to do more for back and neck comfort than any single desk, chair or gadget.

slides.headline: Desk-bound and stiff?
slides.body: Our chiropractors look at how you move, suggest practical desk changes and combine hands-on care with exercises you can do at work. Book online — link in bio.

topic: What happens at your first clinical Pilates assessment

slides.headline: What happens at a Pilates assessment?
slides.sub: A step-by-step look at your first appointment.

slides.title: First up: a conversation
slides.body: We ask about your goals, injuries, health history and what you've tried before. Whether it's back pain, getting stronger or returning to sport, this shapes everything that follows.

slides.title: Next: how you move
slides.body: Expect simple tests like squats, balance, bending and rotation, plus checks of strength and flexibility. There's no pass or fail here. We're simply working out where to start.

slides.title: Then: try the equipment
slides.body: You'll try a few exercises on the mat and reformer so you get a feel for the springs, straps and breathing cues. Most people find it gentler than they expected.

slides.title: Finally: your program
slides.body: You'll leave with a plan: whether one-on-one sessions or small classes suit you, which exercises to focus on, and a couple of simple things to practise at home.

slides.title: What to bring and wear
slides.body: Comfortable clothes, grip socks if you have them, and any recent scans or reports. Health fund cover for clinical Pilates depends on your fund and policy, so check with your fund.

slides.headline: When flexibility isn't the thing to train
slides.sub: Why control matters more than range for very bendy bodies.

slides.title: Bendy isn't the same as strong
slides.body: Some people's joints move further than average. That isn't a problem on its own, but it can mean muscles work harder to control the range, which may lead to fatigue or aches.

slides.title: Skip the end-range stretches
slides.body: Many flexible people love sinking into deep stretches. In Pilates, the aim is to work in the middle of your range with control, rather than hanging on your joints at the end.

slides.title: Slow down and feel it
slides.body: Slower movements, lighter springs and smaller ranges help you feel which muscles are working. It can feel oddly harder than big, flowing moves, and that's usually a good sign.

slides.title: Build strength gradually
slides.body: Add load bit by bit with reformer springs, bands and body weight. Research suggests strength training is a helpful part of managing symptoms for many people with hypermobility.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: If joints often feel like they partly slip out, you have widespread pain, or you're unusually fatigued, it's worth chatting with your GP or physio for a proper assessment.

slides.body: Our Pilates team assesses how you move and builds a program focused on control and strength, at a pace that suits you. Book online — link in bio.
